definition: The field that studies how to make a system reach and hold a target by measuring it and correcting it, and how well that works.
The physical thing being controlled, such as a whole drivetrain or an arm, including its weight and friction.
Anything from outside that pushes the system off its course without being commanded, such as a bump from another robot or a heavier load.
A plant, its actuators, its sensors and the code that decides, joined in a loop.
What the actuators actually deliver to the plant, such as the torque from the motors, which can differ from the command the code gave.
The angle where the arc along a circle is exactly as long as its radius. A full turn is 2 pi radians, about 6.28.
A choice of origin and axes that gives numbers their meaning as positions and directions.
A coordinate frame fixed to the field, which stays put as the robot moves.
A coordinate frame attached to the robot, with forward always straight ahead of it.
Changing a quantity to different units by multiplying by a factor equal to 1, such as 25.4 mm per inch.
Where a robot is and which way it faces: x, y and heading together.
Bringing an angle back into a fixed range, such as -180 to 180 degrees, without changing the direction it points.
A way to find which rotation counts as positive: point your right thumb along the axis, and your fingers curl in the positive direction.
The math convention for angles: 0 along the +x axis, and positive counterclockwise.
The value a controller is trying to reach. Another word for the target.
The setpoint minus the measured value: how far the system still has to go, with a sign. Everything a controller does is computed from it.
Swinging back and forth around the setpoint, again and again, instead of settling on it.
Control that measures the result and uses it to decide the next command.
Using a measurement of what a system did to decide what it does next.
The measured quantity a controller is trying to bring to the setpoint.
The command a controller sends to the actuator, such as a motor voltage.
A controller with only two outputs, usually full power and off or full forward and full reverse.
Using different thresholds for switching on and switching off, so a controller doesn't flip rapidly near one value.
How many times per second a control loop runs. A 10 ms delay gives about 100 Hz.
An oscillation that keeps going at about the same size and never dies out, which a controller with only on and off outputs can settle into.
A controller output flipping back and forth very fast, as it does when the error hovers around a switching point.
Control that gets to the target in the shortest possible time with the output limits you have.
A number you choose that sets how strongly a controller reacts. PID has three: kP, kI and kD.
The part of PID that pushes in proportion to the current error.
The part of PID that reacts to how fast the error is changing, acting as a brake.
The part of PID that reacts to the running total of past error, fixing errors that linger.
When the integral term builds up too much while the output is already at its limit, causing overshoot later.
When a controller asks for more than the hardware can deliver, so the output stays at its limit.
How long a system takes to go from 10% to 90% of the way to its setpoint.
How far a system travels past its setpoint.
How long a system takes to get close to its setpoint and stay there.
The error left over once a system has stopped changing.
Finding the gain values that make a controller work well on a particular robot.
A sudden spike in the derivative term caused by the setpoint jumping to a new value.
Output calculated from what you already know the system needs, added before any error appears.
A classic tuning recipe: raise the P gain until the system swings steadily, then compute all three gains from that gain and the swing's period.
A small constant push, in the direction of the error, added so the output is never too weak to overcome friction.
